title: Moving Charges and Magnetism: Biot-Savart Law, Ampere's Law and Magnetic Force
subcategory: Moving Charges and Magnetism — Force on a Charge, Biot-Savart Law, Ampere's Law, Solenoid, Torque

references.label: NCERT Physics Part I, Class 12 — Moving Charges and Magnetism

summary: A magnetic field exerts a velocity-dependent (Lorentz) force on moving charges and a torque on current loops; moving charges (currents) in turn create magnetic fields, described at the small-element level by the Biot-Savart law and, for highly symmetric current distributions, more simply by Ampere's circuital law.
explanation: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field dB due to a small current element Idl at a point: dB = (μ₀/4π)(Idl × r̂)/r², proportional to current and inversely proportional to the square of distance, with direction given by the right-hand (or cross-product) rule — the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law, but for a current ELEMENT rather than a point charge, and always perpendicular to both the current direction and the line to the point. Ampere's circuital law, ∮B·dl = μ₀Ienclosed, is the magnetic analogue of Gauss's law: exactly true always, but a genuine calculation shortcut only for highly symmetric current distributions (long straight wire, solenoid, toroid), where a suitable Amperian loop makes B uniform along the path. The Lorentz force on a moving charge is F = q(E + v×B); the magnetic part, F = qvB sinθ, is zero if the charge is at rest or moving along B, and maximum when moving perpendicular to B — this velocity-dependence is what distinguishes magnetic force fundamentally from the always-present electric force. Since magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, it does NO work on the charge, only changing its direction, not its speed. In a cyclotron, this property is used to accelerate charged particles in a spiral path using a fixed-frequency alternating voltage timed to the particle's circular motion — the cyclotron frequency f = qB/2πm is remarkably independent of the particle's speed or orbit radius (at non-relativistic speeds), which is what makes the fixed-frequency design work. A moving-coil galvanometer detects small currents via the torque a current-carrying coil experiences in a radial magnetic field (τ = NIAB), converted into an angular deflection measured against a calibrated scale.
commonMisconceptions: Applying Ampere's law to a non-symmetric current arrangement expecting an easy answer — like Gauss's law, it is always true but only computationally useful when symmetry makes the line integral tractable.

Assuming magnetic force can change a charged particle's speed — it cannot; being always perpendicular to velocity, it does zero work and only changes direction (unlike an electric force, which can do work and change speed).
Forgetting that a charge moving PARALLEL to a magnetic field feels ZERO magnetic force (sinθ = 0 when θ = 0°), a frequently tested special case.

Assuming two current-carrying wires always attract — they attract only when the currents flow in the SAME direction; opposite-direction currents REPEL, the reverse of the like/unlike rule for electric charges.
examples: A long, straight current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field that circles around it, with magnitude decreasing as 1/r — found quickly via Ampere's law thanks to cylindrical symmetry.
In a cyclotron, protons spiral outward gaining energy each half-turn, but their time per revolution stays constant even as their speed and radius increase.
Two parallel wires 1 m apart, each carrying exactly 1 A in the same direction, attract each other with a force of 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre of length — this is literally how the ampere itself is defined.
genZNote: Magnetic force: does zero work, all vibes — just redirects you without ever changing your speed.

explanationSections.heading: Magnetic Force on a Moving Charge
explanationSections.body: The Lorentz force on a moving charge is F = q(E + v×B); the magnetic part, F = qvB sinθ, is zero if the charge is at rest or moving along B, and maximum when moving perpendicular to B — this velocity-dependence is what distinguishes magnetic force fundamentally from the always-present electric force. Since magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, it does NO work on the charge, only changing its direction, not its speed.

explanationSections.heading: Motion in a Magnetic Field
explanationSections.body: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field travels in a circle (the magnetic force supplies the centripetal force); if it also has a velocity component along B, the path becomes a helix. In a cyclotron, this circular motion is used to accelerate charged particles in a spiral path using a fixed-frequency alternating voltage timed to the particle's circular motion — the cyclotron frequency f = qB/2πm is remarkably independent of the particle's speed or orbit radius (at non-relativistic speeds), which is what makes the fixed-frequency design work.

explanationSections.heading: Biot-Savart Law
explanationSections.body: The Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field dB due to a small current element Idl at a point: dB = (μ₀/4π)(Idl × r̂)/r², proportional to current and inversely proportional to the square of distance, with direction given by the right-hand (or cross-product) rule — the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law, but for a current ELEMENT rather than a point charge, and always perpendicular to both the current direction and the line to the point.

explanationSections.heading: Magnetic Field on the Axis of a Circular Current Loop
explanationSections.body: Integrating the Biot-Savart law over a circular loop of radius R carrying current I gives the field on its axis at distance x from the centre: B = μ₀IR²/[2(R²+x²)^(3/2)], directed along the axis. At the centre itself (x = 0), this simplifies to B = μ₀I/2R — the standard result used as a building block for solenoid and coil problems.

explanationSections.heading: Ampere's Circuital Law
explanationSections.body: Ampere's circuital law, ∮B·dl = μ₀Ienclosed, is the magnetic analogue of Gauss's law: exactly true always, but a genuine calculation shortcut only for highly symmetric current distributions (long straight wire, solenoid, toroid), where a suitable Amperian loop makes B uniform along the path.

explanationSections.heading: The Solenoid
explanationSections.body: Inside a long, tightly-wound solenoid (n turns per unit length carrying current I), Ampere's law gives a uniform field B = μ₀nI parallel to the axis, essentially independent of position as long as you're well inside and away from the ends; the field just outside the solenoid is approximately zero. This uniform-field property is why solenoids are used to create controlled magnetic field regions in electromagnets and inductors.

explanationSections.heading: Force Between Two Parallel Currents; the Ampere
explanationSections.body: Two long parallel wires carrying currents I₁ and I₂, separated by distance d, exert a force per unit length on each other of F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) — currents in the SAME direction attract, currents in OPPOSITE directions repel (the reverse of like/unlike electric charges). This mutual force is used to define the SI base unit the ampere: one ampere is the constant current that, if maintained in two straight parallel infinite wires 1 metre apart in vacuum, produces a force of exactly 2×10⁻⁷ N per metre of length between them.

explanationSections.heading: Torque on a Current Loop; Magnetic Dipole
explanationSections.body: A planar current loop of N turns, area A, carrying current I, behaves as a magnetic dipole with magnetic moment m = NIA (direction given by the right-hand rule, perpendicular to the loop's plane). In an external field B, the loop experiences zero net force but a torque τ = m×B = NIAB sinθ, which tends to rotate the loop until its moment aligns with B — the same principle by which a moving-coil galvanometer detects current.

explanationSections.heading: The Moving Coil Galvanometer
explanationSections.body: A moving-coil galvanometer detects small currents via the torque a current-carrying coil experiences in a radial magnetic field (τ = NIAB), converted into an angular deflection measured against a calibrated scale.
